# How to Spot a Phishing or Scam Message Before You Click

> **In short:** Paste a suspicious email or text into any AI assistant (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, or Le Chat) and ask it to list the warning signs — it's a 30-second second opinion, but always verify with the real company before clicking or paying.

Phishing is when a fake message pretends to be from a real company, courier, or person, hoping you'll tap a bad link or send money. These messages are getting harder to spot. The fake emails look like real bank notices. The scam texts use your real name and address. Before you tap a link or wire money, getting a quick second opinion from an AI takes about 30 seconds — and it can catch things your tired eyes miss.

## Before you start
- A free account on any AI assistant that accepts pasted text — ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, or Le Chat all work for this. No paid plan is needed.
- The suspicious message itself, copied as plain text (you'll do this in Step 1).
- Total time: about 5 minutes the first time, under 2 minutes once it's a habit.
- Important: do NOT click any link inside the suspicious message before starting.

## Step 1 — Don't click anything, just copy the message
Resist the urge to tap a link or reply. On your phone, long-press the suspicious email or text, look for a "Copy" option in the small menu that appears, and tap it. On a computer, click inside the message and press Ctrl+C (Windows) or Cmd+C (Mac). The text lands in your clipboard, ready to paste somewhere safe. If the message is an image rather than text, take a screenshot and save it — many assistants can read screenshots too.
💬 Example: a copied scam text might read "URGENT: Your account will be closed in 24 hours. Verify now at account-verify.example.com."
You'll know it worked when you can paste the message text into any other app (try Notes or a blank document) and see all the words appear there.

## Step 2 — Open any AI assistant in a fresh chat
Open the app or website of an AI assistant you already use, and start a brand-new conversation. A fresh chat matters because you don't want old messages confusing the AI. Look for a button labeled something like "New chat", a "+" icon, or a pencil symbol — usually at the top-left or top-right of the screen. If you don't see any of these, refresh the page or close and reopen the app to start clean.
💬 Example: tap "New chat" in ChatGPT, "New conversation" in Gemini, or refresh claude.ai in your browser.
You'll know it worked when you see a blank message box with no chat history above it.

## Step 3 — Paste the message and ask for a phishing check
Tap inside the empty message box and paste the suspicious text. On a phone, long-press and choose "Paste". On a computer, use Ctrl+V or Cmd+V. Then add a clear instruction telling the AI exactly what you want. Be specific — don't just paste and hope the AI notices something. If the AI's first reply is short or just says "looks fine", ask a follow-up question like "list every warning sign, even small ones" to get a more useful answer.
💬 Example prompt to copy: "I'm pasting a message I received. Please tell me: (1) does it look like a phishing or scam attempt, (2) what specific warning signs do you see, and (3) what should I do before I click anything? Here's the message: [paste it here]"
You'll know it worked when the AI gives you a clear list of warning signs — like urgency, weird sender addresses, or suspicious links — instead of a vague yes-or-no answer.

## Step 4 — Read the warning signs the AI flags carefully
Take 60 seconds to read the response. Most phishing messages share a few classic red flags: pressure to act fast ("within 24 hours"), threats ("your account will be closed"), requests for passwords or money, sender addresses that don't quite match the real company, links with strange domain names (watch for example.com spelled wrong, like examp1e.com or account-verify.example.co), or generic greetings like "Dear Customer" instead of your real name. The AI will usually list three to six specific things it noticed. If it says the message looks safe, that's useful information — but it isn't a green light to click.
💬 Example: an AI might flag three things at once — the urgent tone, the misspelled domain, and the request for your password — which together are a strong scam signal.
You'll know it worked when you have a short list of specific reasons the message looks suspicious (or one clear reason it looks safe) that you can repeat back in plain words.

## Step 5 — Verify independently before doing anything
The AI is a fast first pass, not the final answer. If the message claims to be from your bank, open the bank's official app or type the bank's website address directly into your browser — never through the link in the message. If it's about a delivery, go to the courier's site and enter the tracking number yourself. If someone claims to be a family member in trouble, call them on a number you already have saved. The rule is simple: the AI flags the message, but you confirm with the real source before acting.
💬 Example: if the text says "Your package couldn't be delivered", open the courier's official site in a new tab and type in the tracking number there — don't tap the link in the suspicious message.
You'll know it worked when the real source (your bank, the courier, your family member) either confirms the message is fake, or confirms it's real and the AI just had a false alarm.

## Step 6 — Delete, block, or report the message
Once you've confirmed it's a scam, you have three quick choices. Delete the message so you don't tap it by accident later. Block the sender so they can't reach you again. And if the message pretends to be from a real company, report it. On iPhone, long-press a text and tap "Report Junk"; on Android, tap the three dots next to the message and look for "Block & report spam". In Gmail, open the email, click the three dots at the top, and choose "Report phishing". In Apple Mail, swipe left and tap "Move to Junk". The exact label varies, but look for anything like "Report", "Block", or "Mark as spam".
💬 Example: in Outlook, right-click the email, choose "Security Options", then "Mark as Phishing" — this both reports and removes it.
You'll know it worked when the message is no longer in your inbox and the sender can't message you again from the same address.

## Common mistakes
- **Testing a suspicious link by clicking it.** Even one tap can install malware or steal your login. Never open a link from a message you haven't verified. Type the address yourself if you need to reach the real site.
- **Trusting the AI too much.** AI assistants miss things, especially brand-new scam formats or messages written in your local language. Use the AI as a fast first check, then verify with the real company before acting.
- **Asking the AI to "decide if I should click".** You decide. The AI can list warning signs, but it can't see your real account, your real bank balance, or the actual context. The final click is always yours.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** the next time you get a "your package is delayed" text or a "suspicious login" email, you'll have a 30-second habit — copy, paste into an AI, read the warning signs, then verify directly with the company before doing anything. That one habit catches most scams before they cost you money.
- **For your work or business:** if scam messages are landing in a shared inbox or team channel, paste one into an AI and ask it to summarize the pattern, group similar senders, and draft a short "this was reported as phishing" reply. That turns a pile of scam messages into a 5-minute cleanup task instead of a daily annoyance.
- **If you're just getting started:** save the Step 3 prompt somewhere easy to reach — Notes app, a phone shortcut, a browser bookmark. The next time anything feels off, you have a one-tap habit ready instead of trying to remember what to ask.

## Try it now
Find the most recent suspicious message in your inbox or text history — the one you've been meaning to ignore — and paste it into any AI assistant using the prompt from Step 3. Take 60 seconds to read the warning signs it flags, then decide: delete, block, or report.
